The supply of the necessary foodstuffs and medical supplies for the population of Srebrenica. "2. About safe, speedy, and organised departure of all these people from Srebrenica to Tuzla, including able-bodied men starting with an urgent evacuation of the wounded. This is going to be a major logistical operation that could start as early as on the 13th of July. This policy of the UNPROFOR was implemented by members of the Dutch Battalion. Namely, at the first meeting at the Fontana Hotel Karremans told Mladic that UNPROFOR wished people to be pulled out, i.e., that they were waiting for buses to arrive ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We don't receive English translation at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise. We cannot follow all the references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the last part of the sentence which is recorded is that "they were waiting for buses to arrive ..." From there on you should continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number of the document you are referring to so that it can be brought up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This policy of UNPROFOR was implemented by members of the Dutch Battalion; namely, Karremans at the first meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, I asked you to give the reference again, the number of the document, so that it can be brought up on the screen which would assist the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1008, pages 16 and 17 in Serbian and 19 to 21 and 26 and 27 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And on page 20 of the transcript from this meeting it is said, and I quote: "What I was requested by General Nicolai and something that was ordered to him by General Janvier in Sarajevo as well as by the authorities, to stop what had been going on in the last six days on behalf of the population, and for the benefit of the population, all of us would like to maintain the status quo and then to -- the enclave to be abandoned." In other words, these are the statements made by Colonel Karremans. Therefore, one cannot attribute the forcible relocation of the population to the VRS, having in mind that this operation was carried out at the request of UNPROFOR and the civilian population of the enclave and, at the same time, the Dutch Battalion asked them to abandon and leave the enclave as soon as possible. General Mladic did not want to agree to that before he heard from representatives of the civilian population and he asked for two meetings with them. Tolimir was not in Srebrenica, either on the 12th or the 13th of July or before or after these dates. However, in paragraph 354 the Prosecution says, and I quote: "That officers for intelligence at all levels within the VRS from the Main Staff downwards were under Tolimir's command and they supervised, co-ordinated, and carried out the operation of forcible relocation." This argument is totally unfounded and speculative. First of all, none of the officers or soldiers of the VRS or members of the MUP was under Tolimir's command. Tolimir could not issue any orders to them. During combat operations, all individuals had to operate and follow the orders of the commander of the operation and not Tolimir's proposals. The officers who were present in Potocari and Srebrenica were directly under the command of the operation commander. They couldn't and they didn't receive orders from Tolimir. At the time, Jankovic was resubordinated to the command of the Drina Corps and he served as a liaison officer for UNPROFOR. The Prosecution witness, Colonel Salapura, said in this trial on 3rd May 2011, transcript page 13578, that sometime between the 11th and 19th Radoslav Jankovic was subordinated to the command of the Drina Corps. In other words, everything he did he did pursuant to the orders under the direction and control of the Drina Corps and not of Tolimir. The Prosecution corroborates their argument that Tolimir controlled Jankovic by citing Exhibit P626. First of all, there is no information contained in this document testifying to the fact that Tolimir had any knowledge about any criminal offence committed during the evacuation. On the contrary, in his report Jankovic wrote the following, inter alia: "We believe that we wish to take control of the enclaves Zepa and Gorazde, and in order to do that it is necessary to portray the action in Srebrenica in the media in such a way that we are depicted as providing fair treatment to the population and even to the combatants who laid down their weapons." One can only draw one reasonable conclusion from this. Jankovic has no information about any killing plans. If there was a plan to kill the able-bodied men, how was it then possible to portray it in the media as receiving good treatment? In paragraph 894 the Prosecution asserts that Tolimir supervised, directed, and guided his subordinates, including Jankovic, Popovic, Momir Nikolic, and as well as the military police of the Bratunac Brigade and the Drina Corps, while they were directing a forcible relocation of the population from Potocari on the 12th and 13th of July which was -- and that he was fully aware of the illegality of their actions. This claim of the Prosecution is completely unfounded. First of all, where was Tolimir on the 12th and 13th July? Was Tolimir present at the meetings in the Fontana Hotel or did he participate in any other operation relating to Srebrenica? Tolimir informed the commander of the operation and the security organs about everything he knew about the enemy activities in accordance with the rules of war which is something that is going to be discussed later on in the rebuttal to the accusation about the alleged joint criminal enterprise of killing able-bodied men of Srebrenica. None of the VRS officers who were present in Srebrenica was under Tolimir's command. Tolimir did not supervise their work and he couldn't do that because that was the responsibility of their respective commanders and the operation commander who took part. Since Tolimir was not in Srebrenica on the 12th or 13th July and since he did not take part in the evacuation of the Srebrenica population, as requested by the UN officials, Tolimir cannot be considered responsible for the alleged forcible relocation of the population nor for opportunistic killings cited by the Prosecution in the indictment. The Prosecution has come forward with a series of unfounded accusations against Tolimir with regard to the events in the area of Zepa in July 1995. In paragraph 60(D) of the indictment the Prosecution says, and I quote: "That Tolimir took part in the negotiations with the representatives of Muslims of Zepa and offered them a choice between evacuation or military action by the VRS." This assertion is completely erroneous. In paragraph 895 of their final brief, the Prosecution alleges that Tolimir gave "illegal" ultimatum by saying: "That the population had to leave the enclave or face a military action." The Prosecution qualifies this as a criminal act of forcible relocation. The meeting that the Prosecution qualified in the above-described way was documented in a number of exhibits. First of all, P491 is Tolimir's report dated the 30th of July from the said meeting. It says in the first sentence, and I quote: "On the 13th of July, 1995, at 1200 hours we had a contact a Hamdija Torlak, the president of the Zepa executive committee and Mujo Omanovic, a member of the War Presidency, about the demilitarisation of the enclave and the freedom of movement of the civilian population pursuant to the Geneva Conventions of 12th August 1995." This document does not contain a single reference to any forcible act of forcing the civilian population to leave the enclave. The commander of the Ukrainian Battalion in Zepa was also present at the meeting. This is Prosecution Exhibit P596 which is a memorandum dated 13th July 1995 drafted by Louis Fortin. In paragraph 8 it is said, and I quote: "The commander of the Rogatica Brigade, accompanied by General Tolimir and local representatives, held a meeting at the Ukrainian command post 2 today at 12 00 hours. The Serbs asked the Zepa Bosnians to lay down their weapons, after which the civilian population can either go or stay." And the last sentence of paragraph 9 reads, I quote: "The Serbs want to take hold of this pocket without fighting, if possible." In other words, the ultimatum had nothing to do with forcible relocation of the civilian population. It has been proven in this trial that there were many civilians in Zepa who wanted to leave the enclave. For example, the majority of the population was constituted by refugees who wanted to leave the enclave because other members of their families were either accommodated in other areas or they wanted to leave to third countries. Tolimir reports about these negotiations, which is Exhibit P491, and it reads, I quote: "We have provided guarantees for the evacuation of the entire civilian population and able-bodied men who surrendered their weapons as well as security and safety for the civilian population who decide to acknowledge the authority of Republika Srpska and to remain in its territory." Therefore, this is not about expelling population, but rather allowing the able-bodied men who surrendered their weapons, that is to say members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who wants to leave, to be allowed to leave. Therefore, it is clearly stated that safety will be guaranteed to those who decide to stay behind. This kind of conduct is in compliance with the agreement on demilitarisation of Srebrenica and Zepa from 1993 which was confirmed by an agreement on general cessation of hostilities on 31st December 1994. According to document P145 in which Tolimir reports that the planned contacts were not made, he indicates that the Muslim want, and I quote: "Secure the support of the majority of the population for the already-made decision to move out. They informed most of the inhabitants and soldiers that everybody will be allowed either to leave or to stay in the area of Zepa, provided they surrender their weapons and recognise the Serbian authority." A number of well-off Muslims showed interest to move out with their movable property and to move to the FRY or to -- through third countries, thereby wishing to avoid being engaged in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. With the mediation of UNPROFOR, we informed the Zepa leadership that the process of moving out and the surrender of weapons must commence at 900 hours on the 15th of July, 1995, if they decide not to move out under the offered conditions, we are planning to start combat operations. Therefore, this has nothing to do with the expulsion of the population. It has to do with the demilitarisation of the enclave. It has to do with the evacuation of those who are supposed to lay down their weapons and not about the forcible removal of the civilian population. That's why the accusation contained in paragraph 60 of the third amended indictment is completely without foundation. The objective of the attack on Zepa was not the civilian population as, in fact, indicated in Exhibit P1225. It is a document by General Krstic dated the 13th of July, 1995, titled: "Order to attack the enclave of Zepa." In item 9 of the order you can read the following, and I quote: "The civilian Muslim population and UNPROFOR are not the targets of our forces. They are to be rounded up and kept secure under guard and the armed Muslim groups are to be crushed and destroyed." The orders of this and similar sort are not issued for the sake of formality but to be complied with. As was the case with Srebrenica, the area of Zepa was also passed off as a demilitarised zone and the Muslims routinely cited and exploited as far as they could this abominable lie. As stated by Viktor Bezurchenko in the report entitled: "The Fall of Zepa," which is Exhibit D55, at paragraph 65, and I quote: "The BH army expected Zepa to attract the attention of the international media, and the moral guidance administration of the BH army General Staff had been developing instructions for a psychological operation related to Zepa. It was the strategy of the BH army to deny the presence of any BH army units in Zepa, Srebrenica, or Gorazde, to attribute any military operations to the unarmed population, and not to admit to any or not to accept any discussions on evacuation." The transcript does not state that this was D55, paragraph 65. And let me continue. What was truly going on is indicated in a number of documents that were admitted into evidence in this case and I will cite only several of them. On the 14th of July, 1995, the War Presidency of Zepa issued a decision to call general mobilisation. This is Exhibit D349. Under this decision, all the available resources and personnel were placed in the service of the army. General Petar Skrbic, in answer to a question put by Judge Mindua, stated as follows, and I quote: "This clearly states that all those who are able-bodied should be placed at the disposal of the brigade and will become members of the brigade without any additional conditions. They are to be issued with weapons, their work obligation is to be discontinued, and they are to become full-fledged members of the brigade." The document is also significant because the way in which general mobilisation was called in Zepa and since this applied to able-bodied members of the army, in the case of their capture they would be entitled to the status of prisoners of war. Izetbegovic Alija Izetbegovic, the president of the BH Federation, spoke about the evacuation of Zepa with General Smith. Thus, in document D363, a letter sent by Alija Izetbegovic to General Delic, it is stated and I quote: "I have just finished by talks with General Smith. Perhaps I should secure the evacuation of Zepa, and I mean women and elderly from Zepa with the mediation of UNPROFOR." And item 4 reads, and I quote: "This contains a plan of the evacuation of the population of Zepa which is to be applied in the event that neither the contents of items 1 or 2 are to be feasible. And I am sending you annexed the plan of the evacuation of the population of Zepa. This plan states that it was developed on the basis of the message that was sent out by the people of Zepa on the 16th of July, 1995, and the information provided by the commander of the OS Zepa of the 17th of July, and that it was on the basis of these documents that talks were held with Alija Izetbegovic on the 17th and 18th July 1995. Now, the proposal that this document contains in item 2 is as follows, and it's on the following page, and I quote: "That the entire population of Zepa should be evacuated in an organised fashion in evacuation groups and as soon as may be if possible forthwith, or rather, based on assessments of the situation on the ground in order to ensure their safe transport. The BH army ought to secure the column of the population which is to be evacuated. Those members of the population who are not able to be evacuated on foot for reasons of health or other reasons or to be put up in the UNPROFOR base in Zepa, and once a list of them has been drawn up are to be evacuated with the assistance of the International Red Cross, UNHCR, and other international institutions and transferred to the free territory. These individuals are to be accommodated in the UNPROFOR base in Zepa right away and they should follow the last unit leaving the territory of Zepa in order to ensure the secrecy of the entire evacuation plan."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was the end of the citation of the entire evacuation plan. Mr. Tolimir, it's now time for the second break. I have no idea how much time you will need to conclude your closing arguments. You have one hour left, three-quarters of an hour today and one-quarter of an hour tomorrow. I would like to invite you especially to address the core issues of this case in the remaining hour. As you know, since February of this year, like the Prosecution, you have one day for presenting your final submissions, your oral final closing arguments. Will you be able to finalise it within one hour? This is one question I have for you and I have one question for Mr. McCloskey and then we may know how to proceed. Are you able to indicate already now if you will need time for rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, everyone, Mr. President, Your Honour. Yes, we would like some time for rebuttal. I doubt very much it will take all of the 30 minutes, but we have identified some issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In any case, that makes clear that we are sitting tomorrow with the completion of Mr. Tolimir's submissions, with rebuttal by the Prosecution, and possible rejoinder by Mr. Tolimir. We have our second break now and -- no, first of all, Mr. Tolimir, will you be able to conclude your oral submissions in the remaining hour?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have 24 pages left. My legal advisor and I will try to cut it down unless we are going to be able to present it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In preparing for your oral submissions you should have thought about the length of the presentation, the speed of everything you will present. And I think you know that from February of this year and you were reminded yesterday at the outset of our hearing that you, as the Prosecution, will have one day, no more. Mr. Gajic, I see you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my apologies, a small intervention. As we were preparing the closing arguments, if you look at the word count it roughly corresponds to the word count of the Prosecution's closing arguments and I was guided by that as I was working with Mr. Tolimir on our submissions. Our closing arguments even fall somewhat short of that, that's to say one day's oral submissions by the Prosecution. And I think we are more or less on the track and if we end up short of some 15 to 20 minutes, we will kindly ask for your leave to proceed until the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I will repeat that it is necessary to prepare an oral submission of a reasonable length. Mr. Tolimir, you have indicated that you together with your legal assistant will try to make it short so that we can finish in the time given. We adjourn and resume quarter past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We will skip a portion and I'll say that we are starting from item 127 for interpreters' sake. In a word, it was a plan of the Muslim authorities to evacuate the entire population and you can glean that from the conversation between Alija Izetbegovic and the population of Zepa. Item 129, this exhibit clearly demonstrates, namely D54, that the evacuation had been planned secretly by the BH Federation leadership and that it had been kept secret in order to accuse the VRS of attacking the civilian population and driving them out. Paragraph 130 reading sentence 5: "Benjamin Kulovac and Hamdija Torlak have come as authorised representatives for these negotiations in the manner envisaged under the relevant rules of the Geneva Conventions. At this meeting Hamdija Torlak stated that the best solution would be to evacuate the entire population of Zepa. When asked by General Mladic whether there was anyone who wanted to stay, he answered in the affirmative and said that there were ten families who wanted to stay and this is proved by the video-clip introduced into evidence as D108. I'll now move to paragraph 132. On the other side, on the other hand, the ministry of the foreign affairs of the BH Federation had asked the Security Council back on the 17th of July to carry out the evacuation as corroborated by D107. This is the president's letter to the Security Council dated the 20th of July, 1995, which requests the Security Council to, or rather, this is the release by the Security Council requesting the Bosnian Serbs to co-operate in this matter. Let's move on to 134, Exhibit D58. On the 24th of July, 1995, the agreement on the disarmament of the able-bodied population in the enclave Zepa was signed. The Prosecution deny any importance that this agreement may have, that's at paragraphs 426 to 431. However, from the perspective of international law this agreement is completely valid and in keeping with the Geneva Conventions. Its primary role is to ensure that the Zepa Brigade be disarmed, and as for the civilian population, item 7 of it states, and I quote: "That the civilian population of Zepa shall in keeping with the Geneva Conventions of the 19th of August, 1949, and the Additional Protocol of 1977 be granted the freedom of choice as to whether to stay in the area for the duration of the war conflicts. In other words, nobody was being expelled. It is only a matter of circumstance that the agreement was stipulated in the context of combat activities, but that does not detract from its validity. Let us move on to paragraph 135. The role of Tolimir. During the evacuation of Zepa was to work on the implementation of the 24 July agreement and to make sure that the evacuation is without any incidents. Tolimir was in the centre of Zepa escorting the convoy together with the commander of the Zepa Brigade, Avdo Palic. And now we move on to paragraph 138, this is for the benefit of the interpreters. The participation of Tolimir in the implementation of the evacuation of the population of Zepa in keeping with the agreement which was signed on the 24th of July, 1995, the evacuation of the civilian population, including some military able-bodied men, cannot be considered participation in any criminal enterprise. Contrary to what the Prosecution alleges in paragraph 60 under D1 of the indictment, Tolimir made sure that the evacuation of Zepa was carried out without any problems in keeping with the agreement that was signed on the 24th of July, 1994 [as interpreted]. When it comes to the evacuation of the population of Srebrenica, in that evacuation Tolimir did not play any role. He did not participate in it. The only thing that he suggested was to make a list of all military able-bodied men, including those that were to be evacuated from the Potocari base. In keeping with Alija Izetbegovic's plan, the civilian population was indeed evacuated from Zepa in a safe manner and the BiH army did not lay arms, but rather they continued fighting. General Smith on page 11597 of the transcript testified that in Belgrade Carl Bildt negotiated about the transfer of the Zepa Brigade across the river Drina into Serbia. This is also mentioned in Viktor Bezurchenko's report entitled: "The Fall of Zepa." This is Exhibit D55. Ramo Cardakovic led the transfer to Serbia. He was the Chief of Staff the 285th Brigade. The Prosecutor treats that transfer of the Zepa Brigade as a crime of deportation which is charged in the indictment. Exhibit D111 is the list of those who had crossed the Drina and who had been treated as prisoners of war in the Republic of Serbia. You can see in this list that all those were military able-bodied men who had been army members. For a crime of deportation it is necessary for those persons who crossed the border, resided legally in the territory of Zepa; however, their stay in Zepa was illegal, it was contrary to the agreement of the demilitarisation of the enclave, according to Article 5 of the agreement on the demilitarisation of Zepa. They should not have been allowed to enter or stay in the demilitarised zone. Additionally, they crossed over to Serbia of their own choice in agreement with UNPROFOR members and the government in Serbia. And they were guided by the representative of the international community Carl Bildt. There is no single piece of evidence based on which one might conclude that the VRS wanted to expel them across the border. For those reasons the conditions for deportation as a crime against humanity have not been fulfilled. In the last paragraph of D488 it is stated, and I quote: "We believe that the destruction of the convoys of Muslims from Stublic and Radava, Brloska Planina the Muslims would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just was reminded that this is a confidential document. When you quote from this document you should be aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand. What document is confidential? D111. Very well. I apologise. Well, you can protect it. I did not understand that it was a protected document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is D488 you asked or you referred to when you started to quote from it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be P488. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. That's clarified the situation, P488. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the last paragraph of that document it is stated: "We believe that the destruction of the convoys of the Muslim population from the directions of Stublic, Radava and Brloska Planina the Muslims would be forced to surrender quickly ..." First of all, when it comes to convoys, we're not talking about the civilian population but about a destruction of those features that might be used for -- as hiding places for the population. For example, caves, different areas on the ground. Mirko Trivic testified about that on transcript pages 8625 and 8626. The word "convoy" does not refer to the evacuees but the features on the ground that may be used for hiding, so Tolimir does not suggest that the population should be destroyed as it is ascribed to him, but rather places where the evacuees could hide. Paragraph 152 for the benefit of the interpreters. When it comes to the alleged participation of Tolimir in the alleged joint criminal enterprise - and we are talking about the killing of militarily able-bodied men in Srebrenica - the Prosecution bases its allegation on Tolimir's position as the assistant commander for security and intelligence. However, when it comes to Zdravko Tolimir's participation in the alleged operation of the killings of prisoners of war, there is no evidence to that effect. There can be no credible evidence. In the course of this trial, not even the witnesses who struck a plea -- a bargain with the Prosecution about the admission of guilt did not charge Tolimir. Paragraph 153. When it comes to the consideration of the charges that Tolimir has been charged with when it comes to the killing of militarily able-bodied men in Srebrenica, it has to be mentioned that Tolimir was engaged in Operation Zepa during that period of time and that there is no single piece of evidence that Tolimir in the relevant time-period at all knew about any operation to kill militarily able-bodied Muslims. Page 54 of the document that I'm reading from, where it says: "In a series of paragraphs the Prosecution alleges," that is the last word in the last sentence, "that Tolimir commanded, controlled, or provided instructions to certain people who were in Srebrenica from the 12th of July onwards." This is not founded at all. There is no single piece of evidence to that effect. During the trial the Prosecution several times referred to P112. This is the instruction on commanding the security organs of the VRS. That instruction was issued in peace time due to the omissions that were observed in the work of the intelligence and security organs. In this document it is stated and I quote: "The security and intelligence organs are under the immediate command of the commander of the institutions to which they belong. In professional terms they are subordinated to their superior commands. When it comes to professional command and control, I'm talking about the issuing -- I'm not talking about issuing orders, but rather the authorities that are vested in any officer and that is to direct the work of the organ and to make sure that they are properly trained. When it comes to the brigade corps, the security organs are independent and they perform the tasks of counter-intelligence and other tasks envisaged by the relevant regulations. The assistant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, let me interrupt you for a moment. You referred to P112. You see on the screen that these are photographs. It should be a different document number. Can you repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The assistant commander of the Main Staff of the VRS does not command. He only professionally guides his troops and works on the tasks entrusted with him by the commander. Otherwise, the principle of the singleness of command would be impaired. When it comes to the control, that can only be professional control, nothing else, and it doesn't imply the control of the organs of the security in the course of combat activities or any other tasks. This is the task of a commander. In order to control the work of the organ of security or any other organ, the person who controls that work has to be present or he has to be provided with appropriate reports also known as the reports of the security organs. They're not sent to Tolimir but to the security administration. Where Tolimir was during the evacuation that he participated in, nobody was killed. As for the rapport between the commander and the security organs, this can be best illustrated by the testimony of the Prosecution witness Keserovic, who said that on the 16th he received an order from General Mladic as a security organ, he received an order from his commander to go on a mission, to abort his regular activities. He could not not obey that. He had to do that. He had to come back and report to the commander. This illustrates the relationship with the commander and the security organs irrespective of who the commander is, irrespective of who is subordinated to whom. Everybody's subordinate to the commander. Professional services have only a professional role that facilitates the implementation of any task. When it comes to the events that ensued after the fall of Srebrenica, there were no such reports at all. There's no evidence that Tolimir was aware of any killing operation at the relevant period and that the reports were sent to him at Boksanica. That was the front line facing the Muslims. That was an UNPROFOR check-point. When negotiations were underway, no reports could be sent there. No reports indeed arrived there. The Prosecution alleges in paragraph 89 of its final brief that Tolimir was the only person in the Main Staff who was authorised and capable of controlling the security organs and controlling them in the implementation of the order to expel the civilian population and the militarily able-bodied men. First of all, Tolimir did not have the right to command over the security organs. Only the commanders had that right, the commanders of the units to which those organs belonged, including Keserovic. Second of all, control means presence at the location where killings are being committed. Tolimir was neither in Srebrenica nor at any other location where the killings were committed. During the Prosecution case, we did not hear any piece of evidence, we did not hear any witness testifying to the fact that Tolimir was informed about the operation to kill militarily able-bodied men. We didn't hear that he issued any proposals, instructions, or any other such thing involving the killing of prisoners of war. The Prosecution alleges that Tolimir, I quote: " ... applied his professional knowledge and skills within the purview of military strategy in order to co-ordinate the work of intelligence and security organs and agents ..." That is in paragraph 2 of the final brief. This also involved -- the military police that were used in order to implement that goal." And this is a reference to objectives contained in the allegation about the joint criminal enterprise. The Prosecution does not have any proof for this allegation. Under the law, Tolimir has no right to command the security/intelligence organs or police organs; they're all subordinated to their respective commanders. We're going back to Keserovic's example, who appeared here as a Prosecution witness, who had to carry out the task given by the commander and then had to come back and report to him and in the process he had to suspend his activities in training police forces. I am reading paragraph 167. In other documents cited by the Prosecution supporting the alleged contribution of Tolimir to the killing operation is the Defence Exhibit D49, which is a document sent by Tolimir from Zepa on the 13th of July, 1995. It clearly confirms that Tolimir had no knowledge whatsoever about the alleged plan for killing prisoners of war. Please, document D49. It clearly shows that Tolimir did not have any knowledge about the alleged plan to kill prisoners of war. In paragraphs 572 to 585, the Prosecution is making a speculation and offering completely unreasonable conclusions. First of all, in this document Tolimir says, and I quote: "If you are not able to provide appropriate accommodation for all prisoners of war from Srebrenica," this part of the sentence indicates that Tolimir is not addressing the issue of the accommodation of prisoners of war in Srebrenica, but that this is being done by somebody else. This sentence only indicates that Tolimir has no responsibility and no duties with respect to prisoners of war of Srebrenica. Secondly, Tolimir insists on appropriate accommodation and that can only be construed as accommodation that would be in compliance with the rules of the Geneva Convention which was explained in the final brief. Tolimir also says that in the facilities of the 1st Light Brigade there are proper accommodation facilities that can house 800 prisoners of war. Witness Carkic on transcript page 12740 testified that the facilities in Sjemec were used for a certain period of time as billeting facilities for one of the Rogatica Brigade units. Therefore, the Prosecution's allegation that the accommodation was not suited for -- to its purpose was unfounded. Thirdly, this document was sent in the evening of the 12th July 1995 at around 10.00. This cannot be interpreted as the fact that Tolimir was informed about the killing operation or about any unlawful treatment of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 13th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the Prosecution's assertions that Tolimir warned about the drone, he in fact informed combat organs that had capacity to destroy such aircraft. In that period, the VRS was under the threat from air attacks. This is document 128 which was sent only to the Drina Corps command and not to intelligence and security organs. As I said, the VRS was in the said period exposed to threat from NATO and therefore the information about drones was something that was regularly provided, which can be seen from Exhibit P1216, issued by Milenko Zivanovic on the 5th of July, 1995, who was the commander of the Drina Corps, which means that this was one day before the commencement of Krivaja operation. The document reads: "Due to the possibility of NATO air-strikes, all subordinate units of the Drina Corps" -- so I repeat. "Due to the possibility of NATO air-strikes and the operations conducted by Rapid Reaction Forces around the enclave, particularly around the enclave of Srebrenica and with a view to providing protection to our forces from air-strikes with the focus in the general area of Srebrenica, all subordinate units of the Drina Corps and all anti-aircraft units within subordinate units as well as the available small arms and common weapons shall be placed at full combat preparedness in order to act in a timely manner against enemy aircraft and thereby be ready to operate with all available weapons to attack helicopters used by Rapid Reaction Forces in order to prevent flights over the front lines and thereby risking the safety of our forces in depth, open fire at aircraft and helicopters without seeking particular approval. The allegation that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Tolimir please repeat for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading paragraph 177. Following a completely unreasonable conclusion contained in paragraph 769 of the Prosecution's final brief in which the Prosecution makes reference to an intercept of the conversation between Tolimir and Popovic has nothing to do with prisoners of war of Srebrenica, namely, I'm talking about P765 which states that Popovic was inquiring about a relative of his who had been taken prisoner. However, the Prosecution extracted only one portion of that intercept and draws from it completely unreasonable conclusion. The relevant portion reads: "Popovic: I am today in my base and I have some things to complete, therefore I remained here. Tolimir is doing his job," which means that Tolimir was in the base and not out on the ground. Now the most striking example of speculative arguments is something that the Prosecution stated in terms of interpreting the words "he's doing his job" as a criminal order. This document clearly shows that Popovic was in his barracks, in his office, and that he spent the whole day there. This conversation cannot be used as proof that Tolimir gave any order to Popovic with regard to prisoners of war of Srebrenica, particularly not what is being cited by the Prosecution in paragraph 775 in their final brief. The Prosecution charges Tolimir for supervising the 10th Sabotage Detachment on the 16th July and 23rd July while they were committing murders in Branjevo and Bisina. First of all, there is no evidence indicating that Tolimir was aware at all with the activities of members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment at any location. Viktor Bezruchenko says that on the 16th of July Tolimir sent information from Zepa. Secondly, the sabotage detachment, as explained earlier, was an independent unit of the Main Staff and it was directly subordinated to the commander. This was testified to by Petar Salapura and Petar Skrbic. There is not a single shred of evidence that Tolimir either commanded or made any decisions with regard to the engagement of this detention.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Detachment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take you up on your offer and I will read the rest of the document, about ten pages tomorrow. Tolimir mentions, or rather, the Prosecutor speculates about Tolimir's participation in the joint criminal enterprise, namely, killings. On page 20, lines 14 and 15, the Prosecutor alleges that Tolimir knew that Beara was in the Drina Corps. In the relevant time-period Beara was subordinated to the Drina Corps and this information is -- was available to all sector members, but Beara did not report to Tolimir. He did not information Tolimir. It is unfounded when the Prosecution alleges that Tolimir supervised Beara and that Tolimir knew what Beara was doing, and this is what the Prosecutor said in the final brief on 27, that Beara called Krstic. Why didn't he call Tolimir? The Prosecution suggests speculatively that he didn't do that for his own reasons. However, Beara could not report to Tolimir because Tolimir never sent him on a mission and he was not accountable to Tolimir for the tasks that he was assigned to. He was subordinated to the Drina Corps and he reported to the Drina Corps. The Prosecution does not have a single piece of evidence about any communication between any of the participants in the events of the killing on the one hand and Tolimir on the other, and he doesn't have a single proof of evidence about Tolimir's activity in that. There is also speculation about Tolimir having criminally prosecuted two members of the Fojnica Brigade for having helped Muslims. There is no single piece of evidence that Tolimir had filed a single criminal report and that he prosecuted any members of the Army of Republika Srpska for having helped Muslims. The security organs are not -- were not involved in criminal prosecution activities through Tolimir. Tolimir was never involved in any legal matters [as interpreted]. It is -- the security organs did that directly in co-operation with the prosecutor's offices.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, I think there is a problem in page 75, lines 23 and 24. I read: "Tolimir was never involved in any legal matters." Is that what you were saying, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tolimir was not involved in filing criminal reports. He never prosecuted anybody. Security organs did not do that through Tolimir. Security organs co-operated with prosecutor's officers. Tolimir was not involved. Security organs co-operated directly with the competent prosecutor's offices and courts. This is what I said in my conclusion if that is what you had in mind when you intervened. Thank you. The Prosecutor in a number of their conclusions referred to the testimony by Milenko Todorovic and his statement that Tolimir had told him that he would come to Batkovic to see 1200 prisoners. Tolimir never said that. Todorovic could never confirm that. He didn't know when he spoke to and who he spoke to. So his allegations are unfounded. Todorovic himself in his testimony on the 20th of April, 2011, when he was faced with the Exhibit D226 on transcript page 13141 said: "Thank God I can finally see the document that shows, or rather, about which we have spoken at such a length." He did not see that the document was issued in 1993. However, he saw that he was issued on the 16th of July. The document was signed by the chief of staff General Manojlo Milovanovic, which points to the fact that Todorovic's recollection about who he had spoken to is not reliable enough. Additionally, Todorovic's commander, Novica Simic, who was also a witness in this case, or rather, in the Popovic case, and his testimony was adopted through 92 quater rule, he testified in the Popovic case and the transcript from that trial was adopted as Exhibit P2756, and the relevant transcript pages are 28565 through 28570. Novica Simic within the context of the topic of prisoners of war from Srebrenica did not mention Zdravko Tolimir. However, he spoke about who he controlled, how he controlled them, who he contacted, and how he made sure that a certain number of prisoners of war were accommodated in the reception centre in Batkovic. I would like to conclude for today, the Prosecutor's assumption that Mladic and Karadzic Tolimir -- ordered Tolimir to manage and control the killing operation is not corroborated by any evidence. It is just an assumption which serves to deceive this Trial Chamber and the general public about Tolimir's participation in these killings. It is true that Mladic and Karadzic never provided Tolimir with any order with regard to the killing of prisoners of war. There's no single piece of evidence to prove that. There cannot be such evidence because it simply did not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, does that conclude your presentation of today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what remains is something that I would like to summarise in 15 or 20 sentences in the ten minutes that you will grant me as you promised, if you think that this would be a good ending to my closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We can't do that today because we are at the limit and we can't sit longer than 7.00, but I think it's for your benefit to conclude your presentation tomorrow. We will have a sitting in tomorrow afternoon and at the beginning you should sum up and conclude your presentation, and then you have some time to think about that again tomorrow in the morning and to finalise your oral presentation. I think it's better than today to rush through the remaining part of your presentation. Would that be acceptable for you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that I will manage to finalise my closing argument tomorrow within 15 minutes. I apologise once again to the interpreters and to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Then we will have the following programme for tomorrow. First the closing of the closing arguments, the remaining part, in 15 minutes; then rebuttal by the Prosecution; if possible, rejoinder by Mr. Tolimir. It's up to you and you may decide tomorrow what to respond to the Prosecution. And that -- in the end we have to deal with some documents which are MFI'd and we have to decide how to deal with them, as I indicated yesterday, and I hope the parties will be prepared to discuss this matter. We adjourn and resume tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
